Pool Light Repair in Tucson, With Safety Before Anything Else

A pool light that flickers, fogs with water, trips the GFCI or simply stays dark is an electrical problem in a pool full of water. Stay out of the water, and call the free line any hour to reach an independent Tucson-area pool company.

Call (520) 372-1083 Warning signs
  1. Home
  2. Services
  3. Pool Light Repair

Pool light repair in Tucson is not like changing a porch bulb. The fixture sits in a sealed pocket in the pool wall, under several feet of water, wired back to a circuit at the house or the equipment pad. When the seal fails or the wiring wears, water and electricity can meet in the one place where people swim. That is why this page puts safety first: the warning signs, the one test every owner should do each month, what a professional repair involves, and what published guides say it costs.

Tucson Pool Cleaning Pro is only a phone line. Nobody from the line touches your light. You call (520) 372-1083, an automated assistant takes down the problem and the area, and the call is passed to a locally owned pool company that works independently in the Tucson area. From there, that company handles the inspection, the price and the repair, and it bills you, not the line.

Why a pool light is electrical work for a professional

The U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC) notes that the National Electrical Code has required ground fault circuit interrupter (GFCI) protection for underwater pool lighting since 1968. A GFCI watches the current on a circuit and cuts the power in a fraction of a second when some of it leaks away, for example into water. The CPSC and the American Red Cross warn that older pools are the biggest concern, because underwater lights may have worn over the years and may not be GFCI protected at all.

The National Fire Protection Association calls the danger electric shock drowning: current in the water can disable a swimmer's muscles so they cannot stay afloat. You cannot see it or smell it.

Stop and keep everyone out of the water if a light is cracked, fogged or loose, if its GFCI or breaker trips again after one reset, or if anyone feels a tingle. Leave the light switched off. Do not open the fixture, pull it from the wall, change the bulb or open any electrical box. Call a qualified professional.

Pool light warning signs and what they can mean

The middle column is the limit of what an owner should do. Everything in the right column is for the professional.

Pool light warning signs, what an owner can safely do and what a professional checks
What you seeWhat you can safely doWhat a professional checks
Water or fog inside the lensTurn the light off and keep swimmers outThe lens gasket, a cracked lens, water in the fixture and cord
Light flickers or dimsTurn it off. Note whether it happens only when the pump or other equipment runs.Bulb or LED module, loose connections, the transformer on low-voltage systems, water intrusion
GFCI or breaker trips when the light comes onReset once. If it trips again, leave it off.Water in the fixture or junction box, a damaged cord, a failing GFCI
Light does not come on at allCheck the light switch or the timer or automation schedule, and whether a GFCI has trippedThe bulb, the switch, the GFCI, the wiring and the transformer
Fixture loose or hanging out of the wallTurn it off and keep everyone out of the waterThe retaining screw, the niche, the cord and the bonding
A tingle or shock in the waterGet everyone out without touching metal rails, shut the light off at the switch if it is safe to reach, and do not swim again until it is checkedThe whole circuit, the GFCI, grounding and bonding of the pool

The monthly GFCI test

This is the one electrical check an owner should do, and the CPSC says to do it at least monthly. Find the GFCI that protects the pool light. It may be a breaker with a test button in the panel or a subpanel, or a GFCI outlet near the equipment pad; a pool professional can show you which one if you are not sure.

  1. Turn the pool light on and keep everyone out of the water.
  2. Press the GFCI's test button. The light should go out right away.
  3. Press reset (or switch the GFCI breaker back on). The light should come back.
  4. If it fails either step, meaning the light stays on when tested or the GFCI will not reset, leave the light off and have it checked before anyone swims at night.

A GFCI that trips by itself is doing its job. It is telling you something on the circuit is leaking current. Resetting it over and over is not the fix.

What a pool light repair involves

A careful technician starts by shutting the power off at the breaker and confirming it is dead before touching the fixture. On many pools the light is held in its niche by a single screw, and the cord is left long enough that the fixture can be lifted out onto the deck while the pool stays full. From there, the repair is usually one of these:

  • Lens gasket or sealThe rubber ring that keeps water out of the fixture hardens with age and heat. A new gasket, and sometimes a new lens, stops the leak if the inside has not been damaged.
  • Bulb or LED moduleA failed bulb is replaced inside the sealed fixture, then the fixture is resealed and tested.
  • LED conversionAn old incandescent fixture is swapped for an LED fixture that fits the existing niche.
  • Cord and nicheA cord that is cracked or has wicked water, or a damaged conduit, may mean pulling a new cord or replacing the fixture.
  • Low-voltage systemsLights run through a listed transformer add the transformer itself as something to test.

After any repair, the technician should test the GFCI, check the bonding and run the light long enough to be sure the seal holds. Light niches are also a common place for a pool to leak water, so if the level drops and stops at the light, read pool leak and line repair.

Who is allowed to do the work

Fine for the owner

  • Switching the light on and off
  • Checking the light's timer or automation schedule
  • Testing the GFCI monthly and resetting a trip once
  • Looking at the light from the deck for fog, cracks or a loose fixture
  • Keeping swimmers out until it is checked

Leave to a qualified professional

  • Removing the fixture from the niche
  • Opening the lens or changing the bulb
  • Anything inside a junction box, transformer, panel or breaker
  • New cords, new fixtures and LED conversions
  • Testing bonding and grounding

In Arizona, the Registrar of Contractors' R-6 license for pool service and repair leaves out electrical work beyond the first disconnect. The ROC's residential electrical classification is R-11. So before a light repair, ask the company which parts its own license covers and whether an electrical contractor will handle the wiring.

Look up the contractor license. Contractor licensing in Arizona is handled by the state Registrar of Contractors, known as the ROC. A residential R-6 license, Swimming Pool Service and Repair, is the one meant for servicing home pools and making minor repairs; building a pool or replacing a whole plaster or pebble interior falls under construction licenses such as B-5. Whether a cleaning-only route needs any license is not spelled out by the ROC, so it is fair to ask a company what it holds. Write down its ROC number and enter it in the state's license lookup (new tab), which lists the license status, classification and recent complaints. Tucson Pool Cleaning Pro does not run this check on anyone.

Pool lights and Tucson summers

Night swimming is part of a Tucson summer, because evenings stay warm: National Weather Service normals put the average July low at Tucson International Airport at about 76 degrees. That means the light gets more use in the same months its gasket is baking in pool water warmed by afternoon highs near 100 degrees. It is a good reason to test the GFCI each month through the summer and to look at the lens whenever the pool is clear and calm.

Monsoon season, set by the National Weather Service in Tucson as June 15 through September 30, carries lightning as well as rain and dust. Get out of the pool when you hear thunder, whatever the state of the light, and wait until the storm has passed. After a storm knocks the power out, check the light's timer or automation clock, since an outage can reset it.

Questions to ask before a light repair

  • What is wrong with the light: the seal, the bulb, the cord or the circuit?
  • Can the fixture be serviced, or does it need replacing?
  • Who does the electrical part, and which ROC license does that person hold?
  • Will you test the GFCI and the bonding when you finish?
  • If I switch to LED, will the new fixture fit my existing niche?

Common questions

Who repairs pool lights near me in Tucson?

Pool lights are serviced by pool repair companies and by electricians, and some jobs need both. In Arizona the R-6 pool service and repair license does not include electrical work beyond the first disconnect, so ask any company who will handle the wiring side and which license that person holds. The free line can connect you with a Tucson-area pool business that is independently owned; after that, check its license on the Registrar of Contractors search.

Is it safe to swim if the pool light is not working?

If the light is simply dark and nothing else is wrong, the risk is low, but a dark light has no way to tell you whether it is safe. Do not swim if the lens is cracked or full of water, the fixture is loose in its niche, the GFCI or breaker for the light keeps tripping, or anyone feels a tingle in the water. Turn the light off, keep everyone out and have it checked.

How often should I test the GFCI for my pool light?

The U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission advises testing permanently installed GFCIs at least once a month. Press the test button; the protected circuit should shut off. Press reset to restore it. If it does not trip when tested, or will not reset, leave the light off and have a qualified professional check it.

Can a pool light be changed to LED?

Often, yes. Many older incandescent pool lights can be replaced with LED fixtures, and low-voltage lights powered through a listed transformer are also available. Whether your niche, cord and wiring suit a particular fixture is a question for the professional doing the work, who should also test the bonding and the GFCI afterward.

How much does pool light repair cost?

Angi's 2026 pool repair guide lists about $65 to $150 per light for a gasket or conduit seal repair, and roughly $625 on average to replace a whole fixture, with LED replacements at $700 to $1,500. These are national published ranges, not prices from the line. The company you are connected with quotes its own price after it looks at the light.
